extracted.intended_audience: patent classifiers, patent examiners, patent searchers, and patent information professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and interpretive guidance for assigning and reading International Patent Classification (IPC) places (titles, references, notes, groups, definitions, electronic layer) to ensure correct classification and retrieval of patent technical subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of titles — multipart titles
rubrics_metrics.description: The titles of classification places may use a single phrase or several related phrases linked together; titles may also use two or more distinct parts separated by semicolons, and each part of such a multipart title should be interpreted as a separate title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multipart titles when distinct kinds of subject matter are treated together that cannot conveniently be covered by a single phrase. Example: A41D 10/00 'Pyjamas; Nightdresses' — each part is a separate title.

rubrics_metrics.name: References in titles (bracketed phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: A phrase in brackets appearing in a title is a reference to another place in the Classification and shows that the subject matter indicated by the reference is covered by the place referred to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A01F 7/00 'Threshing machines (with flails A01F 9/00)'. Bracketed references point searchers/classifiers to where certain subject matter is actually classified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of references — Limitation of scope (limiting reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: A limiting reference specifies subject matter that is taken to another place and thus is excluded from the scope of the classification place where the reference appears, and it indicates where that subject matter is classified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting references are vital for correct use of a place; they exclude subject matter that would otherwise fit the place. Example: group A01F 7/00 excludes certain items and points to the place covering them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of references — Indication of precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: A precedence reference states that another place 'takes precedence' when subject matter is classifiable in two places or when different aspects are covered by different places, and it is desired that such subject matter be classified in only one place; precedence references are a form of limiting reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedence references most frequently occur at subgroup level and may be replaced by notes at higher levels when several groups are affected. Example: group A01B 35/00.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of references — Guidance (informative reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Informative references indicate for information where to find related subject matter that could be of interest for searching but which is not within the scope of the classification place where the reference occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informative references facilitate search but do not limit scope. Example: group A61H 33/14. Informative references are increasingly moved to the electronic layer to preserve scheme readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting vs informative references in schemes and electronic layer
rubrics_metrics.description: Limiting references are included in both printed classification schemes and the electronic layer in different formats; informative references are progressively removed from printed schemes and transferred to the electronic layer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For up-to-date informative references and explanatory material, consult the electronic layer (hyperlinks) rather than relying solely on printed schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of references relative to title parts
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is usually placed at the end of the title to which it belongs; if the title has multiple parts, the reference is placed after the last part to which it relates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptionally a reference may not relate to all preceding parts but context will make that clear. Example: A47C 'CHAIRS (seats specially adapted for vehicles B60N 2/00); SOFAS; BEDS (upholstery in general B68G)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of references following titles
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference following the title of a class, subclass or group relates to all hierarchically inferior places under that title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a reference is placed after a group title it applies to the group and its subgroups unless context indicates otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: References in guidance headings or notes apply to covered groups
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference in a guidance heading or note relates to all the groups covered by that guidance heading or note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret such references as applying across the set of groups covered by the heading/note, not just the immediate title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed intra-subclass references abbreviate subclass mention
rubrics_metrics.description: In printed versions, a reference from one group to another in the same subclass quotes only the number of the latter group without repeating the subclass code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: B62L 3/00 'Brake-actuating mechanisms (actuating mechanisms for back-pedalling brakes 5/00; Bowden mechanisms F16C 1/10)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoted group usually most relevant but not exhaustive
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a group is quoted in a reference it is usually the most relevant group but not necessarily the only relevant group; hierarchically related groups should also be borne in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searchers should consider quoted groups as pointers, and also examine related hierarchically adjacent groups for completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation rules for multiple items referred to same place
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two or more items of subject matter are referred to the same place, they are separated by a comma and the classification symbols of that place are given only at the end of that reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A01M 21/00 'Apparatus for destruction of unwanted vegetation, e.g. weeds (biocides, plant growth regulators A01N 25/00)'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation rules when items referred to different places
rubrics_metrics.description: References relating to different items of subject matter referred to different places are separated by a semicolon and are to be read independently; exception when substantial wording is common, then common wording is given once with different symbols separated by commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of independent readings: A01K 1/00 'Housing animals; Equipment therefor (building construction, features of buildings E04; ventilating buildings F24F)'. Example of common wording: A01H 3/00 with multiple cited subgroup numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes — purpose and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes define or explain specific words, phrases or the scope of places, or indicate how subject matter is classified; notes may be associated with a section, subsection, class, subclass, guidance heading or group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes clarify terms used in titles or establish relations between places; examples given include definitions following subclass or section titles (e.g., F42, B22F, B01J 31/00).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes override general guidance for associated places
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes apply only to the places concerned and their subdivisions, and override any general guidance in case of conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Note (1) following the title of subclass C08F overrides the Note following the title of section C. Treat local notes as authoritative for their scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indication of changes vs previous editions — italics and edition brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: In this edition, text in italics indicates entries that are new, changed in wording or hierarchical position (affecting scope), or deleted relative to the previous edition; italics entries new/changed are followed by the edition number in square brackets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An Arabic numeral in square brackets (e.g., [4] or [7]) at the end of an entry shows the edition where the entry was new or changed relative to the preceding edition. Deleted group symbols from previous editions appear with italic indications of where subject matter transferred to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advanced-level electronic revision indications
rubrics_metrics.description: In the advanced (electronic) level, entries created or changed after publication are indicated in italics; deleted group symbols appear with indications of transfer; a six-digit number in square brackets (e.g., 2006.03) indicates year and month of an advanced-level revision amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the electronic advanced level for post-publication changes and their dates; italics and date codes signal later amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic layer contents — additional data
rubrics_metrics.description: The electronic layer contains data not reproduced in printed version: classification definitions, informative references, chemical formulae, graphic illustrations and other explanatory data intended to enhance understanding and ease of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access the electronic layer via hyperlinks from scheme text to view richer explanatory material and search aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of classification definitions — clarification not scope change
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification definitions are recommended to clarify exact boundaries of classification places and provide additional information, but they do not change the scope of classification entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use definitions to determine precise boundaries; remember they are explanatory. Where available, definitions are structured and include definition statements, interpretations, and special classifying rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structured format of classification definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification definitions follow a structured format with a definition statement giving a detailed explanation of the scope; they use relevant words/phrases alternative to those in the title and include explanation of limiting/informative references, special classifying rules, and definitions of terms used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions help map words used in patent documents to the classification place and guide searchers to correct places even when terminology differs from titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informative references in electronic layer do not limit scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Informative references in the electronic layer indicate locations of subject matter of interest for searching and do not limit the scope of the associated classification places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informative references are available via hyperlinks in classification definitions for main groups and subgroups and are search aids only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of chemical formulae and graphic illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Chemical structural formulae and graphic illustrations are included where necessary in the scheme (limited use) and more extensively in the electronic layer to define or illustrate classification scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In chemical areas, structural formulae may define scope (e.g., C07D 499/00). Many additional formulae and graphic illustrations are accessible online as examples and explanatory aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of main groups in a standardised sequence (electronic option)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative standardised sequence of main groups (from more complex to less complex and from specialised to non-specialised subject matter) is provided in the electronic layer; users may choose display in numerical order or standardised sequence via hyperlinks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standardised sequence in the electronic version to aid classification by complexity/specialisation when that perspective is helpful for searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'covered' or 'provided for'
rubrics_metrics.description: When subject matter is stated to be 'covered' by/in a classification place, it means the subject matter has characteristics enabling it to be classified in that place; 'provided for' has the same meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A41F 18/00. Interpret 'covered'/'provided for' as indicating classification eligibility based on characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'not otherwise provided for' and 'Other...' groups (residual subject matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression 'not otherwise provided for' means 'not provided for in any other group in the same subclass or in any other subclass'. Groups worded '... not provided for in groups...' cover subject matter not provided for in stated groups; 'Other...' groups cover subject matter not provided for in other related groups at same hierarchical level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many subclasses include a residual main group typically at the end of the subclass to cover subject matter within the subclass scope not covered by other main groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Groups for combination subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Main groups designating subject matter '... covered by more than one of main groups...' provide for subject matter consisting of combinations of characteristics not covered as a whole by any single one of the specified groups; similar wording can also cover subject matter not covered by any group in a specified range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these combination groups when the invention embodies multiple characteristics that individually map to different groups but together are not covered by a single group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and use of 'i.e.'
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression 'i.e.' has the sense of 'equals' and joins two phrases that are to be considered equivalent; one phrase constitutes a definition of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'i.e.' as defining equivalence. Example: A01D 41/00 'Combines, i.e. harvesters or mowers combined with threshing devices'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and use of 'e.g.'
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression 'e.g.' does not limit the preceding phrase but provides examples; it may (a) give a typical illustration; (b) draw attention to definitely included matter; or (c) indicate matter covered by a group for which no dependent subgroup is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'e.g.' as illustrative only, not restrictive. Examples: A42C 5/00 'Fittings or trimmings for hats, e.g. hat-bands' and B62B 7/00 'Carriages for children; Perambulators, e.g. dolls’ perambulators'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical connectors: 'A and B', 'A or B', 'Either A or B, but not both'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A and B' requires the presence of both A and B in the same example; 'A or B' implies presence of A or B or both; 'either A or B, but not both' implies presence of A or presence of B but not both in the same example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret titles and subgroup statements according to these logical meanings when determining whether an example falls within a place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'in general', 'per se', and 'specially adapted for'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'In general' indicates items considered for their characteristics disregarding specific application; 'per se' concerns the item itself as opposed to combinations of which it is part; 'specially adapted for' indicates items modified or particularly constructed for a given use or purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: F16K valves (in general); reference to 'semiconductor detectors per se H01L 31/00' vs combined devices G01T 3/08; A47D 'FURNITURE SPECIALLY ADAPTED FOR CHILDREN'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'or the like'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Or the like' emphasises that the classification place is not limited to the specific subject matter named but also covers similar subject matter with essentially the same characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A01D 3/00 'Non-abrasive sharpening devices for scythes, sickles, or the like' — interpret broadly to include analogous items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of places must be read within superior places
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of any classification place must always be interpreted within the scope of all its hierarchically superior places; section/subsection/class titles are broadly indicative and do not precisely define scope, while subclass and group titles (with associated references/notes/definitions) aim to define scope more precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always consider the context up through section, subsection, class and subclass when assigning or interpreting a place; main group and subgroup titles are subject to this hierarchical constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective scope of a subclass — combined determinants
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective scope of a subclass is defined by, taken together: (a) the subclass title; (b) any limiting references following the subclass/class title; (c) limiting references appearing in groups or guidance headings within the subclass; and (d) any notes or definitions under the subclass title or related higher titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting references can substantially alter subclass scope (example: A47D excludes school benches/desks by reference to A47B); check all these elements collectively to determine the subclass scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subclassification — titles of subclasses include main groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The titles of subclasses sometimes do not embrace the titles of all main groups under them, but the scope of a subclass should be understood to include all subject matter specifically stated in the titles of its main groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume subclass title wording exhaustively lists contents — inspect main group titles for additional covered subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main group scope determined within subclass and by references/notes
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective scope of a main group is determined by its title as modified by any relevant references or notes associated with the main group or with any guidance heading covering it; main groups must be read within the scope of their subclass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance headings are generally informative and do not modify group scope unless context makes it clear; limiting references in guidance headings always modify scope. Example: F04D guidance headings where context indicates differing group scopes for similar titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgroup scope — hierarchical interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a subgroup is to be interpreted within the effective scope of its subclass, main group and any higher indented subgroup; the subgroup's scope is determined by its title as modified by associated references or notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read subgroup titles as specific specialisations of the higher group (examples given for B64C stabilising surfaces and successive indented subgroup readings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgroups extract well-defined portions of a group's field
rubrics_metrics.description: When a group is subdivided, each dependent subgroup covers a particular part of the field covered by the higher group; a subgroup is devised to take out of that field a well-defined portion which can serve as a self-contained field of search. The parent group is used for subject matter within its scope but not specified in any subgroup indented under it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subgroups as focused search targets; if an item fits no subgroup, classify in the parent group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential characteristics determine subgroup scope relative to higher group
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of any subgroup compared with its higher group is determined by the presence of one or more essential characteristics specified in the subgroup title; these may be characteristics not expressed in the higher group title or already expressed there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: H01F 5/00 'Coils' vs H01F 5/02 'wound on non-magnetic supports' (essential characteristic not in higher group); B01D 35/00 vs 35/30 (essential characteristic already expressed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose of Classification — single most relevant place
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of the Classification is to facilitate retrieval: one and the same technical subject should be classified in, and retrievable from, one and the same place — the place most relevant to be searched for that subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify technical subjects in the place most logical for retrieval, considering function vs application orientation and the 'thing' involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between invention information and additional information
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent documents contain 'invention information' (technical information representing an addition to the state of the art, determined using claims, description and drawings in context) and 'additional information' (non-trivial technical information that does not itself represent an addition to the state of the art but may be useful for searching); rules for selection of classification symbols are the same for both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether disclosed subject matter is an addition to the state of the art (invention information) or complementary (additional information); both are classifiable using the same rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of technical subjects of inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical subjects may represent processes, products, apparatus or materials (or their use/application); these categories should be interpreted in their widest sense (examples provided for each).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include polymerisation/fermentation (processes), chemical compounds/fabrics (products), installations/tools/machines (apparatus), and ingredients of mixtures (materials). Apparatus can also be regarded as a product depending on context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify technical subject as a whole where possible; constituent parts may also be invention information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Classification is designed to ensure that any technical subject with which an invention is essentially concerned can be classified as a whole where possible; however, constituent parts may also constitute invention information if they themselves represent novel and unobvious additions to the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer classifying the whole technical subject when the invention concerns it as an entity; if a constituent part is itself novel, it may merit separate consideration/classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-oriented vs application-oriented places — definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Places may be function-oriented (characterised by intrinsic nature or function, independent of particular field of use) or application-oriented (things specially adapted for a particular use; particular use or application; incorporation into a larger system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function-oriented places: e.g., F16K valves by function. Application-oriented places: e.g., A61F 2/24 mechanical valve specially adapted for insertion into a human heart, or B60G for incorporation of a leaf spring into vehicle suspension. Recognise that places are not always exclusively one or the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-absolute nature of function vs application orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: A given place may be more function-oriented than another but less so than a third; places are not strictly binary and can include both function- and application-oriented aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example comparisons: F02F 3/00 (pistons for combustion engines in general) is more function-oriented than F02B 55/00 (rotary type pistons) but less function-oriented than F16J (pistons in general). Consider relative degree when choosing place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of accurately identifying technical subject(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of great importance to identify accurately the technical subject(s) with which each invention is essentially concerned — consider whether the thing involved is the object itself, a special adaptation for a use, or the arrangement/incorporation into a larger system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: For disclosed 'pistons', determine whether the invention concerns the piston itself, a special adaptation for particular apparatus, or the arrangement of pistons in an engine; this determines choice between function- and application-oriented places.

rubrics_metrics.name: When invention information relates only to a particular field of use, prefer application-oriented places
rubrics_metrics.description: Often invention information relates only to a particular field of use; application-oriented places are intended to cover completely the classification of such matter; function-oriented places embrace a wider concept where constructional or functional characteristics are applicable to more than one field of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the disclosure is clearly tied to a particular use or apparatus, prefer the application-oriented place covering that use; otherwise consider function-oriented places.
